Chicago Address Report Card

How an address rates on transit, walkability and daily needs.

Each measure is rated from its Good limit. Walking and train measures have their own Great and Fair cutoffs, which scale if you change the Good limit; the two boxes below apply to the percentile (crime) measures. The overall rating is a weighted average, so a measure with a higher weight counts for more.

How this is calculated

Where does the data come from?

CTA L stops, Metra stations, Chicago Public Library branches, Chicago Park District parks (and their indoor facilities) and a list of grocery stores are built into this page. The address lookup (OpenStreetMap's Nominatim) and walking routes (OpenStreetMap's Valhalla) need an internet connection.

What does the map show?

The address pin, the walking route (or a dashed straight line if the route service is unavailable) to the nearest train station, library, park, grocery store and indoor rec space, and the other places of each kind nearby. Tap a marker for its name. Use the checkboxes under the map to turn layers on and off. The Crime by block group layer shades the census block groups within about a mile (your address's block group has a dark outline). Each is colored by its reported incidents per 1,000 residents in the latest full year, from the lightest yellow (lowest quarter of Chicago residents) to dark red (top 10%). Tap one for its residents and incidents. The home button (house icon) returns to your address. Drag to move the map, and use the + and - buttons, the mouse wheel, or two fingers to zoom.

How are the neighborhood and community area found?

The address is matched to the City of Chicago's neighborhood boundaries, which are simplified in this page, so an address within about a block of a boundary can show the neighboring area. If an address is just outside every boundary, the page shows the nearest neighborhood and says "near".

What is the Community explorer tab?

A reference view of all 77 Chicago community areas, with a switch between Crime and Demographics. In Crime, the map shades each area by reported incidents per 1,000 residents (or by how that rate changed since the first year), with filters for violent, property and other crime and a year picker. Violent covers homicide, sexual assault, robbery, battery, assault, kidnapping and trafficking. Property covers theft, burglary, vehicle theft, criminal damage and arson. Other covers weapons, trespass, stalking and similar offenses. Drug, liquor, fraud and similar categories are excluded. Hatched areas have under 10,000 residents, so their rates are less reliable. In Demographics, pick a measure (income, rent, home value, age, education, commuting and more) and the map and ranking switch to it. Tap an area, or a row in the ranking, for its numbers and a full profile.

What is in the community profile?

The address check shows a profile card for the address's community area: income, rent, home value, share of renters, housing cost burden, education, age, population change, commuting and car access, with each area's rank among the 77 and a citywide comparison, plus the mix of race and ethnicity and ages. These are estimates for the whole community area, mostly from the 2020-2024 American Community Survey, so they describe the area on average and not a particular block. Small areas have wide margins of error. The profile is not rated, because what counts as good depends on what you are looking for.

Credits

Train stops, library branches, park boundaries, neighborhood boundaries and reported-crime data come from the City of Chicago Data Portal (Chicago Transit Authority, Chicago Public Library, Chicago Park District, City of Chicago and Chicago Police Department). Metra station locations are from Metra's published data. The grocery store list was supplied by the site owner. Community area boundaries are from the City of Chicago Data Portal. Community area populations and demographic estimates (2020-2024 American Community Survey and other sources) are from the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning (CMAP) Community Data Snapshots. Address search (Nominatim) and walking routes (Valhalla) are © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License. Street map tiles are from Esri (default) or OpenStreetMap. Election results (November 5, 2024) are from the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners, matched to the City's ward-precinct boundaries.

How are walking times measured?

The page finds the three closest places of each kind in a straight line, asks for a real walking route to each, and uses the shortest. If the route service can't be reached, it estimates from straight-line distance (x1.3 for streets, at 4.8 km/h) and marks the result "(estimated)". For parks, the walk is to the nearest point on the park's boundary.

What do Great, Good, Fair and Bad mean?

Good means within the limit set for that measure. Great means well inside it: within half the limit by default. Fair means over the limit but within the Fair multiplier (1.5 times by default). Bad means beyond that. The card shows the cutoffs for each level. Change any limit, or the Great and Fair multipliers, under Limits.

How is the overall rating decided?

The overall rating is a weighted average, so one weak measure does not sink an otherwise strong address. Each rated measure scores 100 for Great, 75 for Good, 50 for Fair and 0 for Bad, and the scores are averaged using each measure's weight. By default the walk to a train station counts 3, crime counts 3 (as one measure: its three views are combined first, half from your block group and a quarter each from the surrounding block groups and the community area), the library counts 2, and every other measure counts 1. A Bad on a minor measure barely moves the result, while a Bad on crime or transit pulls it down a lot. The average then becomes a rating: 88 or more is Great, 65 or more is Good, 45 or more is Fair, and anything lower is Bad. The score out of 100 is shown next to it, along with the count of Great, Good, Fair and Bad measures. A measure that couldn't be checked, or that is information only, is left out. Change the weights under Limits.

How is "downtown by train" estimated?

It adds the walk to the nearest station to a ride estimate from that station to Clark/Lake in the Loop. The ride is a distance-based estimate (distance x1.2, at about 30 km/h for the L and 45 km/h for Metra), not a schedule. It leaves out waiting and transfers, so tools like Google Maps will usually show a longer time.

What counts as an indoor rec space?

Chicago Park District parks that have indoor recreation: a community center, gymnasium, gymnastics room, indoor pool, fitness center, boxing gym, climbing wall or indoor handball court. Private venues, such as climbing gyms and pickleball facilities, can be added to the list but are not included yet. Walks are measured to the nearest point on the park boundary, not to the building door.

How is crime measured?

Reported incidents in three groups (violent, property and other) in the latest full calendar year are totaled for the census block group the address is in (a block group has roughly 600 to 3,000 residents) and divided by its 2020 Census population. That gives incidents per 1,000 residents, ranked against every other Chicago block group, counting each resident once. A lower percentile is better. The rating uses the percentile (Great at 25 or below, Good at 50 or below, Fair at 75 or below, with the default settings). Violent covers homicide, sexual assault, robbery, battery, assault and kidnapping. Property covers theft, burglary, vehicle theft, criminal damage and arson. Other covers weapons violations, trespass, stalking, intimidation and similar. Drug, vice and fraud reports are left out because they reflect enforcement or are not tied to where a person lives. Only the address's own block group is used, with no neighbors added, so a block group that holds a busy shopping street or a park can show a high rate per resident and a small block group can swing from year to year. Population is from the 2020 Census, so places that have changed since then can be off. Incident locations are rounded to the block for privacy, and reports reflect what is reported as well as what happens. It describes an area, not your personal risk.

What about the surrounding block groups?

The second view in the Crime card adds up the block groups that share an edge with yours (usually four to seven) and works out incidents per 1,000 residents across all of them, then ranks that against the same combined neighbors around every other Chicago block group. Neighbors with no residents, such as parks, are left out, and neighbors outside Chicago are not in the data.

What is crime per resident?

The third crime measure looks up which of Chicago's 77 community areas the address is in and divides that area's reported incidents in the latest full year by its population (2024 estimate). The rate per 1,000 residents is ranked against all 77 community areas, with the same percentile ratings as the other two crime views. Community areas are large and can contain both safer and rougher blocks, so read it together with the half-mile views. Areas with few residents but many visitors, such as the Loop, show a high rate per resident.

How is the crime trend calculated?

The trend compares the total number of incidents in the address's block group in the latest full year with the first year in the data, next to the same change for the whole city. If the area changed less than the city, it improved relative to the city even when the raw number went up. With fewer than 20 incidents in either year the page says the numbers are too small to judge, because small counts swing a lot from year to year. Partial years are not used.

What are the limitations?

The lists are snapshots and can go out of date. The grocery list may be incomplete. Park distances are approximate because park outlines are simplified to points about 15 meters apart. The nearest station on foot isn't always the fastest way downtown.
